newsitem.title: CHINA: China lauds new breed of officials before congress.
newsitem.headline: China lauds new breed of officials before congress.

text.p: China's Communist Party on Monday launched a series of articles leading up to a crucial congress, praising the business acumen of a new generation of officials and urging them to build closer ties with the masses.

In the last five years, the communists had wrought a new breed of officials who were younger, better educated and more business-savvy than their predecessors, the party mouthpiece, the People's Daily, said in a commentary.

The commentary was the first in a planned series leading up to the 15th Communist Party Congress expected in September or October that will pit state president and party chief Jiang Zemin, 69, against left-wing hardliners eager to slow market-style economic reforms.

"Our party has obtained historic results in the task of replacing old cadres with new, vigorously raising excellent young cadres and obviously improving the age structure of leading groups," the commentary said.

The party congress, held once every five years, is to chart the course of the world's most populous nation as it heads into a new era without late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping or other veterans of the revolutionary generation of Mao Zedong.

China's abandonment of Stalinist central planning in favour of capitalist-style reforms launched by Jiang's mentor, Deng, had placed new demands on those who would lead the country into the next century, it said.

"While grasping the important area of building leadership groups, construction of a corps of talented business managers and technical personnel has also received a high degree of attention the last few years," it said.

Communist Party officials in the past were often chosen for their class backgrounds or "red" credentials rather than ability or education, with intellectuals and businessmen scorned as exploiters of the working class.

The commentary gave credit to Jiang, who has struggled to consolidate his grip on power since Deng's death last February, for cracking down on a wave of official corruption and weeding out crooked or complacent cadres.

"In upholding strict party discipline... we should use the unfolding of positive education and the struggle against corruption to further raise awareness of clean government among officials at all levels," it said.

China's economic reforms have given officials unprecedented opportunity to profit from political clout, and Jiang has made the anti-graft battle one of his hallmarks, saying corruption is a virus that could threaten party rule.
Party leaders should also seek closer ties with the masses, the commentary said.

"Officials who seek ease and comfort, don't want to do base work, look down on testing by difficult circumstances, or who cannot become one with the masses, overcome difficulties or solve problems, cannot be promoted or given important jobs," it said.

China propaganda tsar Ding Guangen last week called on state media to back Jiang before the congress and amid revelations of factional strife among the party elite that analysts say marked the start of a campaign to discredit leftists.

At the upcoming congress, Jiang was expected to try to push ahead with unpalatable reforms of the ailing state sector that could push many flagging firms towards bankruptcy and boost the role of private and collective enterprises.
Leftists are opposed to watering down the role of the state sector and have sought to use Marxist theories to battle Deng's sweeping reforms.
